title: Cap. VII: Garissoles Resp. 2 — the dubium and ἐφ᾽ ᾧ as Adam's imputed reatus
pass_a_gloss: Garissoles's first reply ends there. His second targets the doubt readers might feel. He says Paul would have no lawful answer if Paul answered as Placeus wants. The doubt is how Adam's one sin can doom everyone. The answer Garissoles rejects is: because each person sinned in his own person. Placeus calls that playfulness, not a real reply. Personal sinning can explain why people are doomed; it does not explain why Adam's one act has the force to produce death. A fitting reply must talk about Adam's sin, not about each person's sin—which the posed doubt never mentioned. So Garissoles requires reading ἐφ᾽ ᾧ πάντες ἥμαρτον as Adam's own sin whose guilt comes down on all, or which imputation makes common to all. He thinks this so obvious that Placeus must have rushed. Placeus answers that the fourth argument's author may have moved quickly but not too quickly—he argues well— while Garissoles, here as often, argues badly.
pass_b_english: This was Doctor Garissoles's first response. 2. "As to the doubt," he says, "which could arise in readers' minds, there would plainly be no legitimate response of the Apostle if he gave such a one as the learned man wants. For this is the doubt: how there is so great force in one sin of one Adam that it sentences the whole multitude of men to death. The response is said to be that this comes about thence, that all have sinned in their own person. But this is to play, not to satisfy the doubt. For this reason can indeed be why all are sentenced to death, because all have sinned. But here it is not asked why all are sentenced to death, but rather this: why in one sin of one Adam there is so great force that it produces this effect, namely death. The response therefore ought to deal with that sin of Adam, not with each of ours, about which nothing had been said in the doubt proposed. Therefore, for the response to be fitting, it is necessary that we interpret ἐφ᾽ ᾧ πάντες ἥμαρτον of Adam's own sin, which sentences all to death because its reatus descends upon all, or because through imputation it becomes common to all. This is so clear and evident that here the disputant must have been in a great hurry." The author of this reason may perhaps have hurried, but not too much: for he disputes excellently. But whether Doctor Garissoles hurried, I do not know; this much is certain to me, that he here, as elsewhere throughout, does not dispute rightly.
source_text: Haec prima fuit D. G. responsio. 2. Ad dubium, inquit, quod emergere potuit in lectorum animis, nulla esset plane Apostoli responsio legitima, si talem daret, qualem vult Vir Doctus. Dubium enim hoc est, quomodo tanta sit vis in uno unius Adami peccato, ut totam hominum multitudinem morti addicat. Responsio dicitur esse, id inde fieri, quod omnes peccaverint in sua propria persona. Hoc vero ludere est, non dubio satisfacere. Nam haec quidem ratio esse potest, propter quam morti omnes addicantur, quia omnes peccarunt. Sed hic non quaeritur, quare omnes morti addicantur, verum hoc potius, cur in uno unius Adami peccato tanta vis sit, ut hunc effectum producat, nempe mortem. Responsio igitur debet agere de peccato illo Adami, non de nostro uniuscujusque, de quo nihil dictum fuerat in dubio proposito. Itaque ut apposita sit responsio, necessarium est, ut illud ἐφ᾽ ᾧ πάντες ἥμαρτον, interpretemur de peccato ipsius Adami, quod omnes morti addicat, propterea quod ejus reatus in omnes descendit, sive quia propter imputationem commune sit omnibus. Hoc ita clarum est & evidens, ut hic oporteat valde festinasse disputatorem. Festinavit quidem fortasse autor hujus rationis, sed non nimis: optime enim disputat. Sed an festinaverit D. G. nescio, illud certe mihi constat, eum hic, ut alibi passim, haud recte disputare.
